The presence of white blood cells in urine has been noted as a urogenital system abnormality. 3. In the Treating to New Targets (TNT) study, which included 10,001 subjects aged 29–78 years (19% women; 94.1% Caucasians, 2.9% Blacks, 1.0% Asians, and 2.0% others) with clinically evident coronary heart disease (CHD), participants were treated with either atorvastatin 10 mg daily (n=5,006) or atorvastatin 80 mg daily (n=4,995). Serious adverse reactions and treatment discontinuations due to adverse effects were more frequent with the higher dose. 4. Persistent elevations in transaminases (≥3× the upper limit of normal [ULN] on two occasions within 4–10 days) occurred in 62 individuals (1.3%) in the atorvastatin 80 mg group and in 9 individuals (0.2%) in the atorvastatin 10 mg group. 5. Elevations in creatine kinase (CK) levels (≥10× ULN) were rare overall but were more frequent in the high-dose atorvastatin group (13 cases, 0.3%) compared to the low-dose group (6 cases, 0.1%). 6. In the Stroke Prevention by Aggressive Reduction in Cholesterol Levels (SPARCL) study, which included 4,731 subjects aged 21–92 years (40% women; 93.3% Caucasians, 3.0% Blacks, 0.6% Asians, and 3.1% others) without clinically evident CHD but with a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) within the previous 6 months, participants were treated with atorvastatin 80 mg (n=2,365) or placebo (n=2,366) for a median follow-up of 4.9 years. 7. Persistent hepatic transaminase elevations (≥3× ULN on two occasions within 4–10 days) were more frequent in the atorvastatin group (0.9%) compared to the placebo group (0.1%). 8. Elevations in CK levels (>10× ULN) were rare but occurred more frequently in the atorvastatin group (0.1%) compared to the placebo group (0.0%). 9. Diabetes was reported as an adverse reaction in 144 subjects (6.1%) in the atorvastatin group and 89 subjects (3.8%) in the placebo group. 10. In a post-hoc analysis, atorvastatin 80 mg reduced the incidence of ischemic stroke (9.2% vs. 11.6%) but increased the incidence of hemorrhagic stroke (2.3% vs. 1.4%) compared to placebo. 11. The incidence of fatal hemorrhagic stroke was similar between the atorvastatin and placebo groups (17 vs. 18 cases, respectively). 12. Non-fatal hemorrhagic strokes were significantly more frequent in the atorvastatin group (38 cases) compared to the placebo group (16 cases). 13. Subjects with a history of hemorrhagic stroke at study entry appeared to be at increased risk for hemorrhagic stroke. 14. There were no significant differences in all-cause mortality between the treatment groups: 216 deaths (9.1%) in the atorvastatin 80 mg group versus 211 deaths (8.9%) in the placebo group. 15. Cardiovascular deaths were numerically lower in the atorvastatin 80 mg group (3.3%) compared to the placebo group (4.1%). 16. Non-cardiovascular deaths were numerically higher in the atorvastatin 80 mg group (5.0%) compared to the placebo group (4.0%). 17. In a 26-week controlled study in pediatric patients (n=140; 31% female; 92% Caucasians, 1.6% Blacks, 1.6% Asians, and 4.8% others), the safety and tolerability profile of atorvastatin 10–20 mg daily was generally similar to that of placebo. 18. 19. Amlodipine has been infrequently associated with gynecomastia, though a causal relationship is uncertain. 20. Post-marketing experience with amlodipine has included reports of jaundice and hepatic enzyme elevations (mostly consistent with cholestasis or hepatitis), with some cases severe enough to require hospitalization. 21. Amlodipine has been used safely in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, well-compensated congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes mellitus, and abnormal lipid profiles. 22. Adverse reactions reported with atorvastatin since its market introduction include anaphylaxis, angioneurotic edema, bullous rashes (e.g., erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis), rhabdomyolysis, fatigue, tendon rupture, fatal and non-fatal hepatic failure, dizziness, depression, peripheral neuropathy, and pancreatitis. 23. Rare reports of immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy have been associated with statin use. 24. Rare post-marketing reports of cognitive impairment (e.g., memory loss, forgetfulness, amnesia, memory impairment, confusion) have been associated with statin use. These cognitive issues are generally non-serious and reversible upon statin discontinuation, with variable times to symptom onset (1 day to years) and resolution (median of 3 weeks). 25. Drug interaction studies indicate that the pharmacokinetics of amlodipine are not altered when co-administered with atorvastatin, and vice versa. 26. Co-administration of amlodipine with cimetidine, grapefruit juice, magnesium and aluminum hydroxide antacids, sildenafil, digoxin, ethanol, or warfarin did not result in significant pharmacokinetic changes. 27. 28. Erythromycin co-administration did not significantly alter amlodipine pharmacokinetics.
